El <code>xor</code> es el que detecta er: xor is what detects errors in almost everything that transmits data. To each group of bits one more is added, the parity bit, which is the xor of all the rest; that way the number of ones is always even. If a bit gets corrupted on the way, the count stops adding up and the receiver knows that datum arrived wrong. It is a circuit of chained xors and nothing else, and it sits inside memories, disks and communication lines. With a single parity bit one error is detected, but you do not know which: to correct you need more, which is what [[av-informacion|error correction]] is about.
El <code>xor</code> merece un párrafo po: xor deserves a paragraph because it is the one that turns up most: it puts out 1 when the inputs differ. Seen another way, it is addition without carry: $0+0=0$, $0+1=1$, $1+0=1$ and $1+1=0$ carrying one. That reading is the one needed in [[maq-sumador|the next topic]].

Que una sola puerta bastara para todo lo: That a single gate sufficed for everything was proved by Henry Sheffer in 1913, in a paper on the postulates of Boolean algebra: that is why nand is sometimes called the “Sheffer stroke”. Charles Sanders Peirce had reached the same result some thirty years earlier, but his work stayed unpublished until 1933 and nobody found out in time. Neither of them was thinking about circuits: they were results about pure logic, obtained decades before anything existed to plug them into. When the time came to make chips, that oddity turned out to be the cheapest way to build them.
